questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: In a certain region, the electric field is expressed as $\vec{E} = \dfrac{3}{5} E_0 \vec{i} + \dfrac{4}{5} E_0 \vec{j}$, where $E_0 = 2.0 \times 10^3 \text{ N C}^{-1}$. Determine the flux of this field through a rectangular surface having an area of $0.2 \text{ m}^2$ that is parallel to the $y$–$z$ plane.
questions.solution:
The surface is parallel to the $y$-$z$ plane, so its area vector points along the $x$-axis.

$\vec{A} = 0.2 \hat{i} \text{ m}^2$

The electric field is given as:

$\vec{E} = \dfrac{3}{5} E_0 \hat{i} + \dfrac{4}{5} E_0 \hat{j}$

The electric flux $\Phi$ through the surface is the dot product of the electric field and the area vector:

$\Phi = \vec{E} \cdot \vec{A}$

$\Phi = \left( \dfrac{3}{5} E_0 \hat{i} + \dfrac{4}{5} E_0 \hat{j} \right) \cdot (0.2 \hat{i})$

$\Phi = \dfrac{3}{5} E_0 \times 0.2$

Substituting $E_0 = 2.0 \times 10^3 \text{ N C}^{-1}$:

$\Phi = \dfrac{3}{5} \times 2000 \times 0.2$

$\Phi = 1200 \times 0.2 = 240 \text{ N m}^2 \text{ C}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: The electric field in a certain region is defined by $\vec{E} = \dfrac{E_0 x}{l} \vec{i}$. Determine the charge enclosed within a cubical volume defined by the planes $x = 0$, $x = a$, $y = 0$, $y = a$, $z = 0$ and $z = a$. Assume $E_0 = 5 \times 10^3 \text{ N C}^{-1}$, $l = 2 \text{ cm}$, and $a = 1 \text{ cm}$.
questions.solution:
The electric field is given by $\vec{E} = \dfrac{E_0 x}{l} \hat{i}$.

The flux through the cubical volume is non-zero only for the faces perpendicular to the x-axis, as the electric field has only an x-component.

At the face $x = 0$, the electric field is zero, so the flux $\Phi_1 = 0$.

At the face $x = a$, the electric field is $\vec{E} = \dfrac{E_0 a}{l} \hat{i}$. The area vector for this face is $\vec{A} = a^2 \hat{i}$.

The flux through this face is $\Phi_2 = \vec{E} \cdot \vec{A} = \dfrac{E_0 a^3}{l}$.

The total electric flux through the cube is $\Phi = \Phi_1 + \Phi_2 = \dfrac{E_0 a^3}{l}$.

According to Gauss's law, the total flux is related to the enclosed charge by $\Phi = \dfrac{q_{\text{enclosed}}}{\varepsilon_0}$.

Therefore, $q_{\text{enclosed}} = \varepsilon_0 \dfrac{E_0 a^3}{l}$.

Substituting the given values $E_0 = 5 \times 10^3 \text{ N C}^{-1}$, $l = 2 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$, $a = 1 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$, and $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \text{ C}^2 \text{ N}^{-1} \text{ m}^{-2}$:

$q_{\text{enclosed}} = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times \dfrac{5 \times 10^3 \times (10^{-2})^3}{2 \times 10^{-2}}$

$q_{\text{enclosed}} = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times \dfrac{5 \times 10^{-3}}{2 \times 10^{-2}}$

$q_{\text{enclosed}} = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 0.25$

$q_{\text{enclosed}} = 2.2125 \times 10^{-12} \text{ C}$

Rounding to one decimal place, the enclosed charge is $2.2 \times 10^{-12} \text{ C}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charge $Q$ is situated at the centre of a cube. Determine the electric field flux through the six surfaces of the cube.
questions.solution:
According to Gauss's law, the total electric flux through any closed surface is equal to the net charge enclosed by the surface divided by $\varepsilon_0$.

The six surfaces of the cube together form a closed Gaussian surface that completely encloses the charge $Q$ placed at its centre.

Therefore, the total electric flux through all the six surfaces of the cube is $\Phi = \dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charge $Q$ is situated at a distance $a/2$ above the centre of a horizontal square surface of edge $a$, as shown in the figure. Calculate the flux of the electric field through the square surface.
questions.solution:
Consider a hypothetical cube of edge length $a$ such that the given square surface forms one of its six faces.

The charge $Q$ is placed at a distance $a/2$ above the center of the square surface, which corresponds exactly to the center of the hypothetical cube.

According to Gauss's law, the total electric flux passing through the closed surface of the cube is given by:

$\Phi_{\text{total}} = \dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}$

Since the charge $Q$ is located symmetrically at the center of the cube, the electric flux is distributed equally among all six identical faces of the cube.

Therefore, the electric flux passing through the given square surface is:

$\Phi = \dfrac{1}{6} \Phi_{\text{total}} = \dfrac{Q}{6\varepsilon_0}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charge $Q$ is distributed uniformly over a rod of length $l$. A hypothetical cube of edge $l$ is positioned such that its centre coincides with one end of the rod. Determine the minimum possible flux of the electric field through the entire surface of the cube.
questions.solution:
By Gauss's law, the electric flux through the entire surface of the cube is given by $\Phi = \dfrac{q_{\text{enclosed}}}{\varepsilon_0}$.

To minimize the flux, the charge enclosed by the cube must be minimized.

The rod has a uniform linear charge density $\lambda = \dfrac{Q}{l}$.

The enclosed charge is $q_{\text{enclosed}} = \lambda l_{\text{enclosed}}$, where $l_{\text{enclosed}}$ is the length of the rod inside the cube.

One end of the rod is fixed at the centre of the cube. To minimize the length of the rod inside the cube, the rod must be oriented along the shortest path from the centre to the surface of the cube.

The shortest distance from the centre of a cube of edge $l$ to its surface is the perpendicular distance to any of its faces, which is $\dfrac{l}{2}$.

Thus, the minimum length of the rod inside the cube is $l_{\text{enclosed}} = \dfrac{l}{2}$.

The minimum enclosed charge is $q_{\text{enclosed}} = \left(\dfrac{Q}{l}\right) \left(\dfrac{l}{2}\right) = \dfrac{Q}{2}$.

Therefore, the minimum possible flux through the cube is $\Phi_{\text\min} = \dfrac{Q}{2\varepsilon_0}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the net charge in a region in which the electric field is uniform at all points.
options: Depends on the magnitude of the electric field
questions.solution:
According to Gauss's law, the net electric flux through any closed surface is given by $\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = \dfrac{q_{net}}{\varepsilon_0}$.

Since the electric field $\vec{E}$ is uniform at all points in the region, it is a constant vector. The net flux through any closed surface in this region is $\vec{E} \cdot \oint d\vec{A}$.

For any closed surface, the vector sum of the area elements is zero, i.e., $\oint d\vec{A} = 0$.

Thus, the net flux is zero, which implies $q_{net} = 0$.

Alternatively, using the differential form of Gauss's law, $\nabla \cdot \vec{E} = \dfrac{\rho}{\varepsilon_0}$. Since $\vec{E}$ is constant, its divergence is zero, giving $\rho = 0$. Therefore, the net charge in the region is zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the flux of the electric field through a spherical surface of radius $R$ caused by a charge of $10^{-7} \text{ C}$ located at its centre and a second identical charge positioned at a distance of $2R$ from the centre, as shown in the figure.
questions.solution:
According to Gauss's Law, the total electric flux through a closed surface is equal to the net charge enclosed by the surface divided by the permittivity of free space ($\varepsilon_0$).

$\Phi = \dfrac{q_{\text{enclosed}}}{\varepsilon_0}$

The spherical surface has a radius $R$. The charge located at the centre is inside the sphere, while the identical charge positioned at a distance $2R$ from the centre is outside the sphere.

Therefore, the net charge enclosed by the spherical surface is only the charge at the centre.

$q_{\text{enclosed}} = 10^{-7} \text{ C}$

The electric flux through the spherical surface is:

$\Phi = \dfrac{10^{-7}}{8.85 \times 10^{-12}}$

$\Phi \approx 1.129 \times 10^4 \text{ N m}^2 \text{ C}^{-1}$

Rounding to appropriate significant figures, we get:

$\Phi \approx 1.1 \times 10^4 \text{ N m}^2 \text{ C}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charge $Q$ is situated at the centre of an imaginary hemispherical surface. By applying symmetry arguments and Gauss's law, determine the flux of the electric field due to this charge through the surface of the hemisphere, as depicted in the figure.
questions.solution:
According to Gauss's law, the total electric flux through a closed surface enclosing a charge $Q$ is given by $\Phi_{\text{total}} = \dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}$.

To find the flux through the given hemispherical surface, imagine a complete sphere of the same radius with the charge $Q$ at its center. The hemispherical surface forms exactly half of this complete spherical surface.

By symmetry, the electric field lines emanate uniformly in all directions from the charge $Q$. Therefore, the electric flux through the hemispherical surface is exactly half of the total flux through the complete sphere.

Thus, the flux through the hemisphere is $\Phi = \dfrac{1}{2} \Phi_{\text{total}} = \dfrac{Q}{2\varepsilon_0}$.
questions.question: A charge $Q$ is situated at the centre of an imaginary hemispherical surface. By applying symmetry arguments and Gauss's law, determine the flux of the electric field due to this charge through the surface of the hemisphere, as depicted in the figure.

Thus, the flux through the hemisphere is $\Phi = \dfrac{1}{2} \Phi_{\text{total}} = \dfrac{Q}{2\varepsilon_0}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A spherical volume has a uniformly distributed charge of density $2.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ C m}^{-3}$. Determine the electric field at a point located inside the volume, at a distance of $4.0 \text{ cm}$ from the centre.
questions.solution:
By Gauss's law, the electric field inside a uniformly charged solid sphere at a distance $r$ from the centre is given by:

$\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = \dfrac{q_{\text{enclosed}}}{\varepsilon_0}$

$E (4 \pi r^2) = \dfrac{\dfrac{4}{3} \pi r^3 \rho}{\varepsilon_0}$

$E = \dfrac{\rho r}{3 \varepsilon_0}$

Substituting the given values, $\rho = 2.0 \times 10^{-4} \text{ C m}^{-3}$, $r = 4.0 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$ and $\varepsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \text{ C}^2 \text{ N}^{-1} \text{ m}^{-2}$:

$E = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-4} \times 4.0 \times 10^{-2}}{3 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12}}$

$E = \dfrac{8.0 \times 10^{-6}}{26.55 \times 10^{-12}}$

$E \approx 3.01 \times 10^5 \text{ N C}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A gold nucleus ($Z = 79$) has a radius of approximately $7.0 \times 10^{-15} \text{ m}$. Assuming its positive charge is uniformly distributed throughout the nuclear volume, determine the strength of the electric field at the surface of the nucleus.
questions.solution:
The charge of the gold nucleus is given by $q = Ze$, where $Z = 79$ and $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.

$q = 79 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$

The electric field at the surface of a uniformly charged sphere of radius $R$ is given by:

$E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q}{R^2}$

Substituting the given values:

$E = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 79 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{(7.0 \times 10^{-15})^2}$

$E = \dfrac{1137.6 \times 10^{-10}}{49 \times 10^{-30}}$

$E = 23.216 \times 10^{20} \text{ N C}^{-1}$

$E \approx 2.32 \times 10^{21} \text{ N C}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A gold nucleus ($Z = 79$) has a radius of approximately $7.0 \times 10^{-15} \text{ m}$. Assuming its positive charge is uniformly distributed throughout the nuclear volume, determine the strength of the electric field at the middle point of a radius.
questions.solution:
Given $Z = 79$, the total charge of the nucleus is $Q = Ze = 79 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.

The radius of the nucleus is $R = 7.0 \times 10^{-15} \text{ m}$.

The electric field inside a uniformly charged solid sphere at a distance $r$ from the center is given by:

$E = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0} \dfrac{Q r}{R^3}$

At the middle point of a radius, $r = \dfrac{R}{2}$. Substituting this into the formula gives:

$E = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0} \dfrac{Q \left(\dfrac{R}{2}\right)}{R^3} = \dfrac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0} \dfrac{Q}{2 R^2}$

Substituting the known values:

$E = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 79 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{2 \times (7.0 \times 10^{-15})^2}$

$E = \dfrac{9 \times 126.4 \times 10^{-10}}{2 \times 49.0 \times 10^{-30}}$

$E = \dfrac{1137.6 \times 10^{-10}}{98.0 \times 10^{-30}}$

$E = 11.608 \times 10^{20} \text{ N C}^{-1}$

$E \approx 1.16 \times 10^{21} \text{ N C}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charge $Q$ is uniformly distributed throughout the material of a hollow sphere with inner and outer radii $r_1$ and $r_2$, as shown in the figure. Determine the electric field at a point $P$ positioned a distance $x$ from the centre, given $r_1 < x < r_2$.
questions.solution:
The total charge $Q$ is uniformly distributed in the volume between $r_1$ and $r_2$.

The volume of the material of the hollow sphere is:
$V = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi(r_2^3 - r_1^3)$

The uniform volume charge density $\rho$ is:
$\rho = \dfrac{Q}{V} = \dfrac{Q}{\dfrac{4}{3}\pi(r_2^3 - r_1^3)}$

To find the electric field at a distance $x$ ($r_1 < x < r_2$), we consider a spherical Gaussian surface of radius $x$ concentric with the hollow sphere.

The charge enclosed by this Gaussian surface is the charge within the volume from $r_1$ to $x$:
$q_{enc} = \rho \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi(x^3 - r_1^3)$

Substituting the value of $\rho$:
$q_{enc} = \dfrac{Q}{\dfrac{4}{3}\pi(r_2^3 - r_1^3)} \times \dfrac{4}{3}\pi(x^3 - r_1^3) = Q \left( \dfrac{x^3 - r_1^3}{r_2^3 - r_1^3} \right)$

According to Gauss's Law:
$\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = \dfrac{q_{enc}}{\varepsilon_0}$

Due to spherical symmetry, the electric field $E$ is constant in magnitude and points radially outward over the Gaussian surface:
$E (4\pi x^2) = \dfrac{Q(x^3 - r_1^3)}{\varepsilon_0(r_2^3 - r_1^3)}$

$E = \dfrac{Q(x^3 - r_1^3)}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 x^2 (r_2^3 - r_1^3)}$
questions.question: A charge $Q$ is uniformly distributed throughout the material of a hollow sphere with inner and outer radii $r_1$ and $r_2$, as shown in the figure. Determine the electric field at a point $P$ positioned a distance $x$ from the centre, given $r_1 < x < r_2$.
questions.explanation:

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charge $Q$ is located at the centre of an initially uncharged, hollow metallic sphere of radius $a$. Determine the surface charge density on the inner surface and on the outer surface. If a charge $q$ is subsequently placed on the sphere, what will be the surface charge densities on the inner and outer surfaces? Also, find the electric field inside the sphere at a distance $x$ from the centre in both situations.
options:
Initial inner and outer densities: $-\dfrac{Q}{4\pi a^2}$, $\dfrac{Q}{4\pi a^2}$
Final inner and outer densities: $-\dfrac{Q}{4\pi a^2}$, $\dfrac{Q+q}{4\pi a^2}$
Electric field: $\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 x^2}$

Initial inner and outer densities: $0$, $\dfrac{Q}{4\pi a^2}$
Final inner and outer densities: $-\dfrac{Q}{4\pi a^2}$, $\dfrac{q}{4\pi a^2}$
Electric field: $\dfrac{Q+q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 x^2}$

Initial inner and outer densities: $\dfrac{Q}{4\pi a^2}$, $-\dfrac{Q}{4\pi a^2}$
Final inner and outer densities: $\dfrac{Q}{4\pi a^2}$, $\dfrac{q-Q}{4\pi a^2}$
Electric field: $\dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 x^2}$

Initial inner and outer densities: $-\dfrac{Q}{4\pi a^2}$, $\dfrac{Q}{4\pi a^2}$
Final inner and outer densities: $0$, $\dfrac{Q+q}{4\pi a^2}$
Electric field: $0$
questions.solution:
When a charge $Q$ is placed at the centre of the uncharged hollow metallic sphere, the electric field inside the conducting material must be zero.

By Gauss's law, a charge $-Q$ is induced on the inner surface of the sphere. Since the sphere is initially uncharged, a charge $+Q$ appears on the outer surface.

Assuming the sphere is a thin shell of radius $a$, the surface charge density on the inner surface is $-\dfrac{Q}{4\pi a^2}$ and on the outer surface is $\dfrac{Q}{4\pi a^2}$.

When an additional charge $q$ is given to the sphere, it resides entirely on the outer surface. The charge on the inner surface remains $-Q$ to maintain zero electric field inside the metal.

The total charge on the outer surface becomes $Q + q$.

The new surface charge densities are $-\dfrac{Q}{4\pi a^2}$ on the inner surface and $\dfrac{Q+q}{4\pi a^2}$ on the outer surface.

For a point at a distance $x$ from the centre inside the cavity ($x < a$), a spherical Gaussian surface encloses only the central charge $Q$. The uniform charge distributions on the spherical shell do not contribute to the electric field inside the cavity.

Applying Gauss's law, $E (4\pi x^2) = \dfrac{Q}{\varepsilon_0}$, which gives $E = \dfrac{Q}{4\pi\varepsilon_0 x^2}$. This electric field remains the same in both situations.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider a very rough model of a beryllium atom. The nucleus consists of four protons and four neutrons, confined to a small volume of radius $10^{-15} \text{ m}$. The two $1s$ electrons form a spherical charge cloud at an average distance of $1.3 \times 10^{-11} \text{ m}$ from the nucleus, while the two $2s$ electrons form another spherical cloud at an average distance of $5.2 \times 10^{-11} \text{ m}$ from the nucleus. Determine the electric field at a point just inside the $1s$ cloud.
questions.solution:
By Gauss's law, the electric field at a distance $r$ from the center of a spherically symmetric charge distribution depends only on the net charge enclosed within a sphere of radius $r$.

For a point just inside the $1s$ cloud, the distance from the nucleus is $r = 1.3 \times 10^{-11} \text{ m}$. Since the point is just inside the electron cloud, the sphere of radius $r$ encloses only the nucleus. The electron clouds are outside this radius and do not contribute to the enclosed charge.

The beryllium nucleus contains $4$ protons, so the enclosed charge is $q = +4e = 4 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C} = 6.4 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$.

The electric field is given by:

$E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q}{r^2}$

Substituting the given values:

$E = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 6.4 \times 10^{-19}}{(1.3 \times 10^{-11})^2}$

$E = \dfrac{57.6 \times 10^{-10}}{1.69 \times 10^{-22}}$

$E \approx 34.1 \times 10^{12} \text{ N C}^{-1} = 3.4 \times 10^{13} \text{ N C}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Consider a very rough model of a beryllium atom. The nucleus consists of four protons and four neutrons, confined to a small volume of radius $10^{-15} \text{ m}$. The two $1s$ electrons form a spherical charge cloud at an average distance of $1.3 \times 10^{-11} \text{ m}$ from the nucleus, while the two $2s$ electrons form another spherical cloud at an average distance of $5.2 \times 10^{-11} \text{ m}$ from the nucleus. Determine the electric field at a point just inside the $2s$ cloud.
questions.solution:
To find the electric field at a point just inside the $2s$ cloud, we construct a spherical Gaussian surface of radius $r = 5.2 \times 10^{-11} \text{ m}$ centered at the nucleus.

The charge enclosed by this Gaussian surface includes the nucleus and the two $1s$ electrons. The $2s$ electrons lie outside this surface and do not contribute to the enclosed charge.

Charge of the nucleus, $q_n = +4e$
Charge of the two $1s$ electrons, $q_{1s} = -2e$

Net enclosed charge, $q_{enc} = +4e - 2e = +2e$

Using Gauss's law, the electric field $E$ at this distance is given by:

$E = \dfrac{1}{4\pi\epsilon_0} \dfrac{q_{enc}}{r^2}$

Substituting the given values:

$E = \dfrac{9 \times 10^9 \times 2 \times 1.6 \times 10^{-19}}{(5.2 \times 10^{-11})^2}$

$E = \dfrac{28.8 \times 10^{-10}}{27.04 \times 10^{-22}}$

$E \approx 1.065 \times 10^{12} \text{ N C}^{-1}$

Rounding to two significant figures, we get $E \approx 1.1 \times 10^{12} \text{ N C}^{-1}$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Determine the magnitude of the electric field at a point located $4 \text{ cm}$ away from a line charge with a density of $2 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C m}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The electric field due to an infinite line charge at a distance $r$ is given by the formula:

$E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2 \pi \epsilon_0 r} = \dfrac{2k\lambda}{r}$

Given:
Linear charge density, $\lambda = 2 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C m}^{-1}$
Distance, $r = 4 \text{ cm} = 4 \times 10^{-2} \text{ m}$
Coulomb's constant, $k = 9 \times 10^9 \text{ N m}^2 \text{ C}^{-2}$

Substituting the values into the formula:

$E = \dfrac{2 \times 9 \times 10^9 \times 2 \times 10^{-6}}{4 \times 10^{-2}}$

$E = \dfrac{36 \times 10^3}{4 \times 10^{-2}}$

$E = 9 \times 10^5 \text{ N C}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A long cylindrical wire possesses a positive charge with a linear density of $2.0 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C m}^{-1}$. An electron orbits the wire in a circular path, driven by the attractive electrostatic force. Determine the kinetic energy of the electron. (Note that this energy is independent of the orbital radius.)
questions.solution:
The electric field at a distance $r$ from a long cylindrical wire is given by:

$E = \dfrac{\lambda}{2 \pi \epsilon_0 r}$

The electrostatic force on the electron provides the necessary centripetal force for its circular motion:

$\dfrac{m v^2}{r} = eE = \dfrac{e \lambda}{2 \pi \epsilon_0 r}$

$m v^2 = \dfrac{e \lambda}{2 \pi \epsilon_0}$

The kinetic energy of the electron is:

$K = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2 = \dfrac{e \lambda}{4 \pi \epsilon_0}$

Substituting the given values $\lambda = 2.0 \times 10^{-8} \text{ C m}^{-1}$, $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19} \text{ C}$, and $\dfrac{1}{4 \pi \epsilon_0} = 9 \times 10^9 \text{ N m}^2 \text{ C}^{-2}$:

$K = (9 \times 10^9) \times (1.6 \times 10^{-19}) \times (2.0 \times 10^{-8})$

$K = 28.8 \times 10^{-18} \text{ J} = 2.88 \times 10^{-17} \text{ J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A uniformly distributed charge of density $\rho$ is contained within a long cylindrical volume. Determine the electric field at a point $P$ located inside the cylindrical volume at a distance $x$ from its axis, as shown in the figure.
questions.solution:
Consider a coaxial cylindrical Gaussian surface of radius $x$ and length $L$ passing through point $P$.

By Gauss's law, the total electric flux through this surface is:

$\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = \dfrac{q_{\text{enclosed}}}{\varepsilon_0}$

Due to the symmetry of the long cylinder, the electric field $\vec{E}$ is radial and its magnitude is constant over the curved surface of the Gaussian cylinder. The flux through the flat circular ends is zero since the electric field is parallel to them.

$E(2\pi x L) = \dfrac{q_{\text{enclosed}}}{\varepsilon_0}$

The charge enclosed within the Gaussian surface is:

$q_{\text{enclosed}} = \rho \times \text{Volume} = \rho (\pi x^2 L)$

Substituting the enclosed charge into Gauss's law:

$E(2\pi x L) = \dfrac{\rho \pi x^2 L}{\varepsilon_0}$

$E = \dfrac{\rho x}{2\varepsilon_0}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A nonconducting sheet with a large surface area and a thickness $d$ contains a uniform charge distribution of density $ho$. Determine the electric field at a point $P$ located inside the plate, at a distance $x$ from the central plane, and identify the qualitative shape of the graph of $E$ against $x$ for $0 < x < d$.
options: $\dfrac{\rho x}{2\varepsilon_0}$; linearly increasing for $0 < x < \dfrac{d}{2}$, then constant for $\dfrac{d}{2} \le x < d$
$\dfrac{\rho x}{\varepsilon_0}$; linearly increasing for $0 < x < \dfrac{d}{2}$, then constant for $\dfrac{d}{2} \le x < d$
$\dfrac{\rho x}{2\varepsilon_0}$; linearly increasing for the entire range $0 < x < d$
$\dfrac{\rho x}{\varepsilon_0}$; linearly increasing for the entire range $0 < x < d$
questions.solution:
Consider a Gaussian pillbox symmetric about the central plane of the sheet, with cross-sectional area $A$ and extending to a distance $x$ on both sides.

For a point inside the sheet ($0 < x < \dfrac{d}{2}$):
The charge enclosed by the Gaussian surface is $q_{\text{enclosed}} = \rho (2xA)$.
Using Gauss's law, $\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = \dfrac{q_{\text{enclosed}}}{\varepsilon_0}$
$E(2A) = \dfrac{\rho (2xA)}{\varepsilon_0}$
$E = \dfrac{\rho x}{\varepsilon_0}$
Thus, the electric field increases linearly with $x$ for $0 < x < \dfrac{d}{2}$.

For a point outside the sheet ($x \ge \dfrac{d}{2}$):
The total charge enclosed by the Gaussian surface is $q_{\text{enclosed}} = \rho (dA)$.
Using Gauss's law, $E(2A) = \dfrac{\rho (dA)}{\varepsilon_0}$
$E = \dfrac{\rho d}{2\varepsilon_0}$
Thus, the electric field becomes constant for $x \ge \dfrac{d}{2}$.

Therefore, the graph of $E$ against $x$ is linearly increasing for $0 < x < \dfrac{d}{2}$ and constant for $\dfrac{d}{2} \le x < d$.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A charged particle with a charge of $-2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$ is positioned close to a nonconducting plate that has a surface charge density of $4.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C m}^{-2}$. Determine the force of attraction between the particle and the plate.
questions.solution:
The electric field produced by a large nonconducting plate with surface charge density $\sigma$ is given by:

$E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$

The force experienced by a charged particle of charge $q$ in this electric field is:

$F = |q|E = \dfrac{|q|\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$

Substituting the given values $|q| = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$, $\sigma = 4.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C m}^{-2}$, and $\epsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \text{ C}^2 \text{ N}^{-1} \text{ m}^{-2}$:

$F = \dfrac{2.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 4.0 \times 10^{-6}}{2 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12}}$

$F = \dfrac{8.0 \times 10^{-12}}{17.7 \times 10^{-12}}$

$F \approx 0.45 \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A silk thread $10 \text{ cm}$ in length has one end attached to the large vertical surface of a charged nonconducting plate. The thread's other end is tied to a small ball with a mass of $10 \text{ g}$ and a charge of $4.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$. The thread forms an angle of $60^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$ with the vertical in equilibrium. Determine the surface charge density on the plate.
questions.solution:
Let $T$ be the tension in the thread, $E$ be the electric field due to the plate, $m$ be the mass of the ball, and $q$ be its charge.

In equilibrium, the forces acting on the ball in the horizontal and vertical directions balance each other:

$T \sin\theta = qE$

$T \cos\theta = mg$

Dividing the two equations, we get:

$\tan\theta = \dfrac{qE}{mg}$

The electric field produced by a large nonconducting charged plate is given by $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\epsilon_0}$.

Substituting this into the equation for $\tan\theta$:

$\tan\theta = \dfrac{q\sigma}{2\epsilon_0 mg}$

Rearranging for $\sigma$:

$\sigma = \dfrac{2\epsilon_0 mg \tan\theta}{q}$

Given values are $m = 10 \text{ g} = 10^{-2} \text{ kg}$, $q = 4.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$, $\theta = 60^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$, $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$, and $\epsilon_0 = 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \text{ C}^2/\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2$.

$\sigma = \dfrac{2 \times 8.85 \times 10^{-12} \times 10^{-2} \times 9.8 \times \sqrt{3}}{4.0 \times 10^{-6}}$

$\sigma = \dfrac{17.7 \times 10^{-12} \times 0.098 \times 1.732}{4.0 \times 10^{-6}}$

$\sigma \approx 7.5 \times 10^{-7} \text{ C/m}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: One end of a silk thread of length $10 \text{ cm}$ is attached to the large vertical surface of a charged nonconducting plate. The thread's opposite end is tied to a small ball having a mass of $10 \text{ g}$ and a charge of $4.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$. In equilibrium, the thread forms an angle of $60^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$ with the vertical. Determine the tension in the string in equilibrium.
questions.solution:
In equilibrium, the forces acting on the small ball are the weight of the ball $mg$ acting vertically downwards, the electric force $qE$ acting horizontally, and the tension $T$ in the silk thread acting along the thread.

Resolving the tension $T$ into vertical and horizontal components gives $T \cos\theta$ and $T \sin\theta$ respectively.

For vertical equilibrium, the vertical component of tension balances the weight of the ball:

$T \cos\theta = mg$

Substituting the given values $m = 10 \text{ g} = 0.01 \text{ kg}$, $g = 10 \text{ m/s}^2$, and $\theta = 60^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$:

$T \cos 60^{}^{{}^{\circ}} = 0.01 \times 10$

$T \times \dfrac{1}{2} = 0.1$

$T = 0.20 \text{ N}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: One end of a silk thread of length $10 \text{ cm}$ is attached to the large vertical surface of a charged nonconducting plate. The thread's opposite end is tied to a small ball having a mass of $10 \text{ g}$ and a charge of $4.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ C}$. In equilibrium, the thread forms an angle of $60^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$ with the vertical. If the ball is slightly pushed aside and released, determine the time period of the small oscillations.
questions.solution:
In equilibrium, the forces acting on the ball are the tension in the thread $T$, the gravitational force $mg$, and the horizontal electric force $qE$.

From the equilibrium condition, the effective acceleration due to gravity $g_{\text{eff}}$ is the vector sum of the acceleration due to gravity $g$ and the acceleration due to the electric field $\dfrac{qE}{m}$.

The angle made by the thread with the vertical is $\theta = 60^{}^{{}^{\circ}}$. The effective gravity is given by:

$g_{\text{eff}} = \dfrac{g}{\cos \theta} = \dfrac{g}{\cos 60^{}^{{}^{\circ}}} = 2g$

The time period of small oscillations for the pendulum is:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{l}{g_{\text{eff}}}}$

Substituting the given values $l = 10 \text{ cm} = 0.1 \text{ m}$ and $g = 9.8 \text{ m/s}^2$:

$T = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{0.1}{2 \times 9.8}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{0.1}{19.6}} = 2\pi \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{196}}$

$T = 2\pi \left(\dfrac{1}{14}\right) = \dfrac{\pi}{7} \text{ s}$

Using $\pi \approx 3.14$:

$T \approx \dfrac{3.14}{7} \approx 0.45 \text{ s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Separated by a distance of $2.00 \text{ cm}$, two large conducting plates are positioned parallel to one another. An electron released from rest near one plate travels to the opposite plate in $2.00$ microseconds. Determine the surface charge density on the inner surfaces.
questions.solution:
Given the distance between the plates, $d = 2.00 \text{ cm} = 0.02 \text{ m}$, and the time taken by the electron, $t = 2.00 \text{ \mu s} = 2.00 \times 10^{-6} \text{ s}$.

Using the kinematic equation for a particle starting from rest:
$d = \dfrac{1}{2} a t^2$

Solving for acceleration $a$:
$a = \dfrac{2d}{t^2} = \dfrac{2 \times 0.02}{(2.00 \times 10^{-6})^2} = \dfrac{0.04}{4.00 \times 10^{-12}} = 10^{10} \text{ m/s}^2$

The force experienced by the electron in the uniform electric field $E$ is $F = eE = m_e a$.
Thus, the electric field between the plates is:
$E = \dfrac{m_e a}{e} = \dfrac{9.11 \times 10^{-31} \times 10^{10}}{1.60 \times 10^{-19}} = 5.69 \times 10^{-2} \text{ V/m}$

For two large parallel conducting plates with opposite charges, the electric field in the region between them is given by:
$E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\epsilon_0}$
where $\sigma$ is the surface charge density on the inner surfaces.

Solving for $\sigma$:
$\sigma = \epsilon_0 E = (8.85 \times 10^{-12} \text{ C}^2/\text{N}\cdot\text{m}^2) \times (5.69 \times 10^{-2} \text{ V/m})$
$\sigma \approx 5.04 \times 10^{-13} \text{ C/m}^2$

The closest matching option is $5.05 \times 10^{-13} \text{ C/m}^2$.

Answer: $5.05 \times 10^{-13} \text{ C/m}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: As shown in the figure, two large conducting plates are positioned parallel to each other and carry equal and opposite charges with surface density $\sigma$. Determine the electric field to the left of the plates.
questions.solution:
Let the surface charge density on the positive plate be $+\sigma$ and on the negative plate be $-\sigma$.

The electric field produced by a large plane sheet of charge with surface charge density $\sigma$ is given by $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$.

For a point to the left of both plates:
The electric field due to the positive plate is directed towards the left (away from the plate) with magnitude $E_+ = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$.

The electric field due to the negative plate is directed towards the right (towards the plate) with magnitude $E_- = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$.

Since these two fields are in opposite directions, the net electric field is their vector sum:
$E_{net} = E_+ - E_- = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} - \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} = 0$

Therefore, the electric field to the left of the plates is zero.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two large conducting plates are placed parallel to each other and carry equal and opposite charges with surface density $\sigma$. Find the electric field in between the plates.
questions.solution:
Let the surface charge density on the inner surfaces of the positive and negative plates be $+\sigma$ and $-\sigma$, respectively.

The electric field at a point between the plates due to the positively charged plate is directed away from it and has a magnitude:
$E_+ = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$

The electric field at the same point due to the negatively charged plate is directed towards it (which is the same direction as $E_+$) and has a magnitude:
$E_- = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$

Since both fields point in the same direction (from the positive plate to the negative plate), the net electric field between the plates is the sum of their magnitudes:
$E_{net} = E_+ + E_- = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} + \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$

Alternatively, using Gauss's law with a cylindrical Gaussian surface having one flat face inside the conducting plate (where $E=0$) and the other face in the region between the plates:
$\oint \vec{E} \cdot d\vec{A} = \dfrac{q_{enclosed}}{\varepsilon_0}$
$E \cdot A = \dfrac{\sigma A}{\varepsilon_0}$
$E = \dfrac{\sigma}{\varepsilon_0}$

Let the surface charge density of the positive plate be $+\sigma$ and the negative plate be $-\sigma$.

The electric field produced by a single large charged plate with surface charge density $\sigma$ at any point outside it is given by $E = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$.

For a point to the right of both plates:
The electric field due to the positively charged plate (left plate) is directed away from it, i.e., towards the right, with magnitude $E_+ = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$.

The electric field due to the negatively charged plate (right plate) is directed towards it, i.e., towards the left, with magnitude $E_- = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0}$.

Since these two fields are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction, the net electric field to the right of the plates is:
$E_{net} = E_+ - E_- = \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} - \dfrac{\sigma}{2\varepsilon_0} = 0$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two conducting plates $X$ and $Y$, each having a large surface area $A$ (on one side), are positioned parallel to one another. A charge $Q$ is imparted to plate $X$, while the other plate remains neutral. Determine the electric field at a point to the right of the plates.
questions.solution:
Consider the surfaces of the plates as 1, 2 (for plate X) and 3, 4 (for plate Y) from left to right.

The total charge on the system of plates is $Q_{net} = Q + 0 = Q$.

The charge on the outermost surfaces (1 and 4) is equal to half of the total charge:

$q_1 = q_4 = \dfrac{Q_{net}}{2} = \dfrac{Q}{2}$

The charges on the inner surfaces (2 and 3) are equal and opposite:

$q_2 = Q - q_1 = \dfrac{Q}{2}$

$q_3 = 0 - q_4 = -\dfrac{Q}{2}$

The electric field at a point to the right of the plates is the vector sum of the fields due to all four surfaces. Taking the right direction as positive:

$E = \dfrac{q_1}{2A\varepsilon_0} + \dfrac{q_2}{2A\varepsilon_0} + \dfrac{q_3}{2A\varepsilon_0} + \dfrac{q_4}{2A\varepsilon_0}$

$E = \dfrac{1}{2A\varepsilon_0} \left( \dfrac{Q}{2} + \dfrac{Q}{2} - \dfrac{Q}{2} + \dfrac{Q}{2} \right)$

$E = \dfrac{Q}{2A\varepsilon_0}$

Since the result is positive, the electric field is directed towards the right.

$E = \dfrac{Q}{2A\varepsilon_0}$

Since the result is positive, the electric field is directed towards the right.
questions.question: Two conducting plates $X$ and $Y$, each having a large surface area $A$ (on one side), are positioned parallel to one another. A charge $Q$ is imparted to plate $X$, while the other plate remains neutral. Determine the electric field at a point to the right of the plates.
questions.explanation:
Consider the surfaces of the plates as 1, 2 (for plate X) and 3, 4 (for plate Y) from left to right.

The total charge on the system of plates is $Q_{net} = Q + 0 = Q$.

The charge on the outermost surfaces (1 and 4) is equal to half of the total charge:

$q_1 = q_4 = \dfrac{Q_{net}}{2} = \dfrac{Q}{2}$

The charges on the inner surfaces (2 and 3) are equal and opposite:

$q_2 = Q - q_1 = \dfrac{Q}{2}$

$q_3 = 0 - q_4 = -\dfrac{Q}{2}$

The electric field at a point to the right of the plates is the vector sum of the fields due to all four surfaces. Taking the right direction as positive:

$E = \dfrac{q_1}{2A\varepsilon_0} + \dfrac{q_2}{2A\varepsilon_0} + \dfrac{q_3}{2A\varepsilon_0} + \dfrac{q_4}{2A\varepsilon_0}$

$E = \dfrac{1}{2A\varepsilon_0} \left( \dfrac{Q}{2} + \dfrac{Q}{2} - \dfrac{Q}{2} + \dfrac{Q}{2} \right)$

$E = \dfrac{Q}{2A\varepsilon_0}$

Since the result is positive, the electric field is directed towards the right.

questions.q: As shown in the figure, three identical metal plates having large surface areas are positioned parallel to one another. A charge $Q$ is given to the leftmost plate, a charge $-2Q$ is given to the rightmost plate, and the middle plate is left neutral. Determine the charge that appears on the outer surface of the rightmost plate.
questions.solution:
Let the charges on the three plates from left to right be $Q_1 = Q$, $Q_2 = 0$, and $Q_3 = -2Q$.

The total charge on the system of plates is:
$Q_{\text{total}} = Q_1 + Q_2 + Q_3 = Q + 0 - 2Q = -Q$

For a system of parallel conducting plates, the charge appearing on the outermost surfaces of the leftmost and rightmost plates is always equal and is exactly half of the total charge of the system. This is a direct consequence of Gauss's law and the fact that the electric field inside the bulk of the conducting plates must be zero.

Let $q_{\text{outer}}$ be the charge on the outer surface of the rightmost plate. Then:
$q_{\text{outer}} = \dfrac{Q_{\text{total}}}{2} = \dfrac{-Q}{2}$

Thus, the charge that appears on the outer surface of the rightmost plate is $-Q/2$.
